Fact: There are five filing statuses: Single, Married Filing Jointly, Married Filing Separately, Head of Household, and Qualifying Surviving Spouse.
Head of Household status requires paying more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying person.
A qualifying child must be under 19, or under 24 if a full-time student, or any age if permanently disabled.
A qualifying child must live with the taxpayer for more than half the year, with limited exceptions.
A qualifying relative's gross income must be below the annual exemption threshold to be claimed as a dependent.
Only one taxpayer can claim a given dependent in the same tax year.
Married Filing Separately often disqualifies taxpayers from several credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit.
Qualifying Surviving Spouse status can be used for up to two years after a spouse's death if a dependent child lives with the taxpayer.
A taxpayer can be claimed as someone else's dependent even if they also file their own tax return.
Support tests, relationship tests, and residency tests all factor into who qualifies as a dependent.
Divorced parents can only both claim the same child in alternating years if Form 8332 is used to release the claim.
A taxpayer's filing status is determined by their marital status as of the last day of the tax year.
Wages, salaries, and tips are reported to the taxpayer on Form W-2.
Self-employment income is reported on Schedule C and flows to Schedule SE for self-employment tax.
Interest income of $10 or more from a bank is reported on Form 1099-INT.
Dividend income is reported on Form 1099-DIV and can be either ordinary or qualified.
Qualified dividends are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates instead of ordinary income rates.
Unemployment compensation is fully taxable at the federal level and reported on Form 1099-G.
Short-term capital gains from assets held one year or less are taxed as ordinary income.
Long-term capital gains from assets held more than one year get preferential tax rates.
Social Security benefits can be partially taxable depending on the taxpayer's combined income.
Rental income and expenses are reported on Schedule E.
Alimony from divorce or separation agreements finalized after 2018 is not taxable income to the recipient.
Gambling winnings are fully taxable as other income, even if no Form W-2G was issued.
Traditional IRA contributions may be tax-deductible depending on income and workplace retirement plan coverage.
Roth IRA contributions are never tax-deductible, but qualified withdrawals are completely tax-free.
Early withdrawals from a traditional IRA before age 59 and a half generally trigger a 10% additional tax.
Required Minimum Distributions apply to most retirement accounts once the account owner reaches the RMD age set by law.
A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored plan, while an IRA is set up directly by the individual.
Rolling over a retirement account within 60 days generally avoids taxes and penalties on the distribution.
Distributions from a traditional IRA are taxed as ordinary income in the year received.
Roth IRA contributions can be withdrawn tax-free and penalty-free at any time since they were already taxed.
Catch-up contributions let taxpayers age 50 and older contribute more to IRAs and 401(k)s each year.
A SEP IRA lets self-employed individuals and small business owners make larger tax-deferred contributions.
Inherited IRAs generally follow different distribution rules than the original owner's account.
The 10% early withdrawal penalty on IRAs has exceptions, including qualified higher education expenses and first-time home purchases.
Form 1099-R reports distributions from pensions, annuities, IRAs, and other retirement plans.
Excess IRA contributions that aren't corrected in time can trigger a 6% excise tax each year they remain in the account.
Adjustments to income are subtracted from gross income to arrive at Adjusted Gross Income, or AGI.
Traditional IRA deductions and student loan interest are both reported as adjustments on Schedule 1.
Self-employed taxpayers can deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an adjustment to income.
Health Savings Account contributions made outside of payroll are deducted as an adjustment to income.
Educator expenses let eligible teachers deduct a limited amount of out-of-pocket classroom supply costs.
Student loan interest deductions phase out at higher income levels.
Self-employed health insurance premiums can be deducted as an adjustment for qualifying business owners.
Adjustments to income reduce AGI, which in turn can affect eligibility for many credits and deductions.
Alimony paid under a divorce agreement finalized before 2019 can still be deducted as an adjustment to income.
To contribute to an HSA, a taxpayer must be enrolled in a High Deductible Health Plan.
HSA contributions are deductible even if the taxpayer doesn't itemize deductions.
HSA funds used for qualified medical expenses are withdrawn completely tax-free.
Unused HSA funds roll over year to year - there is no use-it-or-lose-it rule like a Flexible Spending Account.
Non-qualified HSA withdrawals before age 65 are taxable and generally hit with a 20% additional tax.
After age 65, HSA funds can be withdrawn for any purpose without penalty, though non-medical withdrawals are still taxed as income.
HSA contributions can come from the account holder, an employer, or both, up to the annual limit.
Family HDHP coverage allows a higher HSA contribution limit than self-only coverage.
Taxpayers choose either the standard deduction or itemized deductions, whichever gives the better tax result.
Itemized deductions are reported on Schedule A and include items like mortgage interest and charitable gifts.
The standard deduction amount depends on filing status and is adjusted annually for inflation.
Medical expenses are only deductible to the extent they exceed a percentage-of-AGI threshold.
State and local tax deductions on Schedule A are capped under current law.
Charitable contributions of cash are generally deductible up to a percentage of the taxpayer's AGI.
Taxpayers who are 65 or older, or blind, get an additional amount added to their standard deduction.
The Qualified Business Income deduction can give eligible pass-through business owners a deduction of up to 20% of qualified income.
Mortgage interest is deductible on Schedule A for acquisition debt up to the current law's limit.
A tax credit reduces tax owed dollar-for-dollar, while a deduction only reduces taxable income.
A refundable credit can reduce tax below zero and generate a refund; a nonrefundable credit cannot.
The Child Tax Credit is a per-qualifying-child credit that phases out at higher income levels.
The Earned Income Tax Credit is a refundable credit aimed at low-to-moderate income working taxpayers.
The Child and Dependent Care Credit helps offset costs paid so a taxpayer can work or look for work.
The American Opportunity Credit covers qualified education expenses for the first four years of postsecondary education.
The Lifetime Learning Credit has no limit on the number of years it can be claimed, unlike the American Opportunity Credit.
The Saver's Credit rewards lower-income taxpayers for contributing to a retirement account.
The Credit for Other Dependents applies to dependents who don't qualify for the Child Tax Credit.
Married Filing Separately status disqualifies a taxpayer from several major credits.
Tax is calculated using either the tax tables or the tax computation worksheet, depending on taxable income.
The Additional Child Tax Credit is the refundable portion of the Child Tax Credit.
The Foreign Tax Credit can prevent double taxation on income already taxed by another country.
Estimated tax penalties can apply when a taxpayer underpays throughout the year, even if they pay in full by the filing deadline.
A taxpayer's resident state generally taxes all of their income, regardless of where it was earned.
A nonresident return is typically filed for income earned in a state where the taxpayer doesn't live.
A part-year resident return applies when a taxpayer moved into or out of a state during the tax year.
Many states offer a credit for taxes paid to another state to avoid double taxation on the same income.
Domicile, not just physical presence, often determines which state a taxpayer is considered a resident of.
Some states have reciprocity agreements that let residents of one state work in another without owing that state's income tax.
A handful of states have no state income tax at all.
Remote workers may owe tax in the state where they physically work, even if their employer is based elsewhere.
The IRS officially opens e-file season each year in late January.
The federal filing deadline for most individual returns is April 15, unless it falls on a weekend or holiday.
Taxpayers can request an automatic six-month extension to file, but an extension to file is not an extension to pay.
The IRS processes most e-filed returns with direct deposit refunds within 21 days.
A Preparer Tax Identification Number, or PTIN, is required for anyone who is paid to prepare federal tax returns.
Form 1040 is the standard individual income tax return used by nearly all U.S. taxpayers.
The IRS uses a progressive tax system, meaning higher portions of income are taxed at higher rates.
Marginal tax rate and effective tax rate are not the same thing - effective rate is almost always lower.
